=== TITLE (HN field, 79 chars, fits ≤80) ===
Show HN: Zonoid – a task graph that remembers, and the benchmark where it backfired
(Alt = the exact messaging-note phrasing "...and the benchmark where memory made agents worse" — 95 chars, will truncate in some clients.)

=== URL FIELD ===
https://github.com/yugao-gaos/zonoid
(Post the repo, not a landing page — README hero + demo GIF is the conversion surface.)

=== FIRST COMMENT (post immediately after submitting) ===
Hi HN, I'm the author.

Zonoid is a local-first task graph and bi-temporal knowledge graph for Claude Code agents. The idea is simple: memory should be a byproduct of doing work, not a separate thing you maintain.

When an agent finishes a task, the task node already holds what it learned — the decision, the constraint, the gotcha. Zonoid mines that, LLM-evaluates it, and injects it into future tasks along typed context edges, under a token budget. So the next run starts with the accumulated findings of every prior run instead of a blank slate. Decisions survive sessions. A pre-tool hook also gates every file edit behind a named task claim, so every change traces to a reason.

Here's the part I didn't expect to be writing. I built a held-out benchmark to check whether the memory actually helps, and early versions of my own ON-vs-OFF numbers were contaminated — the "memory" runs were quietly seeing held-out answers. When I fixed the harness, several of the flattering multipliers I'd been about to put in the README evaporated. I retracted them.

So I'm not going to show you a "2x faster" banner. What survived clean measurement:
